claims.quoted_text: the angles \(\angle BAP\) and \(\angle PAQ\) together form \(\angle BAC\)
claims.explanation: This is false: those two angles form only \(\angle BAQ=2\theta\), while \(\angle BAC\) is the sum of all five equal angles, \(5\theta\).
In triangle \(APQ\), the angle at \(A\) is only \(\angle PAQ=\theta\), not \(\angle BAP+\angle PAQ=2\theta\). The correct angle-sum equation is \(\theta+\angle APQ+\angle AQP=180^\circ\).
\(\angle PAQ\) and \(\angle QAP\) are the same angle, and this equation omits \(\angle APQ\). The correct sum for triangle \(APQ\) is \(\angle PAQ+\angle APQ+\angle AQP=180^\circ\).
The congruence of the two angle triples does not force \(\angle BAC\) to correspond to \(\angle APQ\). Also, \(\angle APQ=180^\circ-2\theta\) came from the incorrect angle-sum equation above.
The angles \(\angle QAR+\angle RAS+\angle SAC\) are adjacent angles at \(A\), forming \(\angle QAC\), not the angle at \(C\). Thus \(\angle BCA\) is not equal to \(3\theta\).
The preceding calculation gave \(\angle B=\frac{-180^\circ}{7}\). Dropping the negative sign is not valid; the expression actually evaluates to a negative angle.
This final value does not follow from the previous line \(\angle B=180^\circ/7\), and it is not the correct answer. The correct measure is \(45/2^\circ=22.5^\circ\).
